title: Can teachers spot a ChatGPT essay?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou reports a simple field test of whether teachers can identify ChatGPT-written essays. Inside a Year 4 writing assessment of about 50,000 pupils, No More Marking added a dummy school of eight ChatGPT essays, handwritten out by volunteers, and offered teachers a prize for flagging them during comparative judgement. Of 112 judgements on those scripts only two flagged ChatGPT, while 107 flags in total were raised, so 105 were wrong, and two human scripts were flagged more often than any AI script. She concludes teachers cannot reliably spot ChatGPT writing from unfamiliar pupils. She is candid that the design does not test whether teachers recognise a change in their own pupils' work, but argues the result still matters for the many assessments marked by strangers.
points: In a large-scale test, 12,595 teachers judging ChatGPT scripts almost never flagged them, so human detection of AI writing from unfamiliar pupils is unreliable.
False positives dominated: 105 of 107 flags were wrong, and two genuine pupil scripts were flagged more than any AI script.
The study is limited to anonymised, unfamiliar writers and says nothing about teachers spotting changes in their own pupils' work.
The finding still matters because much assessment involves markers judging students they do not know.
quotes: We were already running a large-scale Year 4 writing assessment of about 50,000 pupils from about 1,100 primary schools. We created an extra dummy ‘ChatGPT’ school featuring 8 essays that were all written by ChatGPT.

We told our teachers about these 8 scripts, and offered a prize if they could successfully identify a ChatGPT essay when they were judging this task. They could flag up a suspected ChatGPT essay very simply, by clicking on our standard button for recording a comment.
In total, 107 judgements were flagged as ChatGPT. So that means 105 of those flags were wrong.
We feel it is fair to conclude that teachers cannot spot a ChatGPT script, and that ChatGPT does a very good job of producing realistically human writing!
This is an obvious limitation of this task design. A lot of the discussion about ChatGPT plagiarism has been about whether teachers can spot plagiarism carried out by their own pupils.

However, we still think this study is useful, as a lot of assessment does involve markers assessing writing from students they don’t know. And it has also helped us to see if there is something so weird or unusual or inhuman about ChatGPT essays that make them very obvious to identify.
